date_label: Fellow prisoners in Reading; staying with Wilde at Berneval-sur-Mer and introduced to Wilde's friends in June 1897
summary: Arthur Cruttenden was a saddler who had served time in Reading with Wilde. In June 1897, barely a month out of prison himself, Wilde had him to stay at Berneval, set about finding someone who could put him back into trade, and wrote to Reggie Turner twice in one day to introduce him - the second time to add that he sang and wrote songs, and to ask Turner to receive him as a friend rather than a case.

sources.quote: Dear Reggie, I write to you a little line to present Arthur Cruttenden to you. He will tell you all the Berneval news. He really is a nice simple fellow, and a good musician, I find. He sings, and writes songs. I hope you will be able to see him as a friend of mine. He is very sensitive to kindness.
sources.context: The second of two letters Wilde wrote to Reggie Turner on 16 June 1897, this one at 1.15 p.m. From the Café Suisse, Dieppe. The first, earlier the same day from Berneval, calls Cruttenden "a very simple nice fellow" who "has been gentle and unassuming and grateful", and sets out the plan to get him back into business as a saddler. Both are printed on the same page.
sources.supports: Wilde's personal regard for him, and the deliberate attempt to place him socially rather than charitably.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
